newsitem.title: USA: U.S. congressman admits taking illegal contribitions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. congressman admits taking illegal contribitions.

text.p: Jay Kim, the first Korean-American elected to the U.S. Congress, pleaded guilty on Monday to accepting illegal campaign contributions, but said through his lawyer he intended to remain in Congress and run for re-election.

Republican Kim, 58, faces up to three years in jail and fines of more than $400,000 when he is sentenced next October for three federal misdemeanor charges, which included accepting a $50,000 illegal campagn contribution from a Taiwanese businessman.
His guilty plea came as Congressional hearings proceeded on illegal foreign contributions made during the 1996 presidential campaign.
By pleading guilty to misdemeanor charges, Kim can keep his job. Usually Congressmen who are found guilty of felony charges are forced out of the House.

The congressman from the Southern California district of Diamond Bar pleaded guilty to three counts of accepting illegal contributions totalling $145,000 from 1992, when he was first elected to Congress, to 1996, when he won his third term.
His wife June, a sometime campaign worker, pleaded guilty to accepting $38,000 in illegal donations from companies and Kim's campaign committee pleaded guilty to concealing the illegal funds.
Federal District Court Judge Richard Paez set Oct. 23 as the date for sentencing.

Kim made no comment after his guilty plea but his attorney Tom Holliday said "he was a contrite man who was accepting responsibility for his crimes." The lawyer added that Kim had no plans to quit Congress and intended to seek re-election.
Kim's chief of staff Matt Reynolds said the congressman had no plans to quit and added, "September promises to be an extremely busy month for the congressman" in terms of his legislative duties.
Reynolds added that the guilty plea does not trigger action by the House of Representatives's Ethics Committee.
A spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's office said it would recommend no more than six months in jail for Kim, although the judge would have the final say.

Kim pleaded guilty to accepting an illegal $50,000 campaign contribution from a Taiwanese citizen, contributing more that $83,000 in illegal corporate contributions from JayKim Engineers Inc. to his campaign and accepting an illegal $12,000 corporate contribution from Nikko Enterprises Inc.

The U.S. Attorney's office previously obtained convictions against five multinational corporations, which made illegal campaign contributions to Kim's 1992 campaign. Korean Airlines, Hyundai Motor America, Samsung America, Daewoo International America and Haitai America have paid a total of $1.6 million in fines.
